questions.question: Baby-Step Giant-Step (BSGS) trades what for what?
options: Memory for time — O(√q) space, O(√q) time, vs trial's O(q) time and O(1) space
Randomness for determinism — same asymptotic but always correct vs random fail
Time for accuracy — sub-exponential but with bounded false-positive rate per query
Communication for compute — distributes work but assumes a shared lookup oracle
questions.explanation: BSGS uses O(√q) memory and O(√q) time, vs naive O(q). Classic space-time tradeoff.

questions.question: In a group ⟨g⟩ of order q, how many evaluations of g^k does BSGS perform?
options: About 2√q — √q 'baby' steps populating a table, √q 'giant' steps querying it
About q^(1/3) — three-stage breakdown saves an order compared with baby-giant
About log q — one per bit of q using square-and-multiply exponentiation
About q — same as exhaustive search through every possible exponent value
questions.explanation: Pick m = ⌈√q⌉. Baby steps: store {g^j : 0 ≤ j < m}. Giant steps: query h·(g^{−m})^i. Match → x = im + j.

questions.question: Pollard's rho for DLP differs from BSGS how?
options: O(√q) time, O(1) memory — random walk + cycle detection, no large table needed
O(q) time, O(log q) memory — deterministic search with binary-search-like queries
O(log² q) time — polynomial in log q, like AKS for primality testing
O(q^(1/3)) time, O(q^(1/3)) memory — three-way meet in the middle algorithm
questions.explanation: Pollard-rho-for-DLP: random walk x ← f(x), look for collisions via Floyd/Brent cycle detection. Same √q time as BSGS but constant memory.

questions.question: What is Pollard's lambda (kangaroo) algorithm useful for?
options: DLP when x is known to lie in a small interval [a, b]; runs in O(√(b − a)) time
DLP in groups with sub-exponential index calculus, replacing the linear algebra phase
DLP only on elliptic curves of CM-type with extra structure exploited heuristically
DLP combined with the Pohlig-Hellman reduction over smooth-order group factors
questions.explanation: Lambda algorithm: when x is in a small range, two 'kangaroos' (tame + wild) walk pseudo-randomly. Collision recovers x in O(√(range)) — much better than √q if range << q.

questions.question: Pohlig-Hellman reduces DLP in a group of order `q = q₁^a₁ · … · qₖ^aₖ` to:
options: k subproblems of DLP in groups of prime order qᵢ; total time O(∑ aᵢ · √qᵢ)
k subproblems of integer factoring on each prime power qᵢ^aᵢ via Pollard-rho
A single DLP in a group of order ∏ qᵢ, recombined via the Chinese Remainder Theorem
One DLP in a group of order max(qᵢ), since the smaller subgroups give zero info
questions.explanation: Pohlig-Hellman: solve DLP mod each qᵢ^aᵢ separately, CRT-combine. Total dominated by largest prime factor of q. Defense: use prime-order subgroups.

questions.question: Solve `g^x ≡ h (mod p)` for g = 5, h = 8, p = 23 (order p − 1 = 22).
options: x = 9, since 5^9 ≡ 12 (mod 23), failing the discrete log target
x = 11, since 5^11 ≡ 22 (mod 23), the order-2 element distinct from 8
x = 14, since 5^14 ≡ 17 (mod 23), missing the target value 8

questions.question: Why must elliptic-curve DLP-based protocols use a generator of prime-order subgroup, not the full curve group?
options: Otherwise Pohlig-Hellman exploits any small prime factor in the group order to break DLP
Otherwise Pollard-rho fails to detect cycles when the order has small composite parts
Otherwise BSGS table construction overflows on subgroups of size > 2^32 in memory
Otherwise the curve becomes singular and the addition law admits a closed-form attack
questions.explanation: If group order = p·k with small k, Pohlig-Hellman reduces DLP to one in subgroup of order p (still hard) + one of order k (trivial). Use prime-order generators (e.g. Curve25519 uses order 8 · ℓ with ℓ prime; use ℓ-order subgroup, clamp scalars).

questions.question: An attacker uses small-subgroup confinement on a DH server. What's the attack?
options: Send a public key of order k (small) instead of order ℓ; server's response leaks shared secret mod k
Send a malformed public key triggering the server's BSGS routine to time-out and crash
Send a non-curve point passing input validation; addition law leaks the private key bytes
Reuse a known DLP precomputation from a prior session against the new shared parameters
questions.explanation: Subgroup confinement: attacker chooses A of order k. Shared secret K = A^b lives in subgroup of order k. Brute-force k possibilities → b mod k. Repeat over different small k, CRT to recover b. Fix: validate public keys lie in the prime-order subgroup.
